The FOMC’s statement maintains a moderately positive outlook—expecting continued labor-market strength and moderate growth with gradual policy normalization. However, the July 2017 SLOOS points to mixed-to-slightly tighter credit conditions that temper this tone: domestic banks reported weaker demand across CRE segments (construction, land development, multifamily) and consumer credit (auto and credit card), with tighter standards for consumer, auto, and credit card loans; mortgage credit conditions eased in several categories (jumbo, QM, GSE), with home-purchase and HELOC standards largely unchanged; nonfarm nonresidential CRE demand was unchanged. Foreign banks reported tighter standards for C&I (across firm sizes) and CRE, despite stronger CRE demand. Together with earlier concerns about elevated valuations and nonbank vulnerabilities, these SLOOS findings suggest softer credit demand and selective tightening that weigh modestly on the otherwise constructive macro backdrop.
